hypothesis: In a sample of cones of one conifer species sharing a given parastichy arrangement (e.g. 5:8 in Norway spruce), the proportion with right-handed parastichy direction is statistically indistinguishable from 0.5.
pass_criterion: With n ≥ 400 cones of a single species and a single parastichy arrangement, a two-sided exact binomial test of H0: p(right-handed)=0.5 gives p > 0.05, and the observed proportion lies within 0.45–0.55 (Thompson's own 224/467 = 0.48).
fail_criterion: The two-sided exact binomial test gives p < 0.01 with the observed right-handed proportion outside 0.45–0.55, in n ≥ 400 cones of one species and one arrangement.
interpretation: 'Right-handed' and 'left-handed' spirals correspond to the modern chirality of the (generative) spiral: clockwise versus counter-clockwise parastichy direction on a cone, viewed from a fixed end such as the apex. The data must record per-cone handedness together with parastichy numbers. Modern reinterpretation: Thompson's 'nearly equally divided' is operationalised as a binomial test plus a 0.45–0.55 proportion band. The claim is about cones, so leaf or shoot phyllotaxis data (e.g. Calathea) cannot decide it.
no_dataset_reason: Searches found no public dataset recording per-cone parastichy handedness together with parastichy numbers for Norway spruce or any other conifer. The Andrews Forest TV019 cone dataset records cone production, not handedness. The only repository-backed phyllotaxis chirality data found was a figshare deposit from a Calathea study, which covers leaf phyllotaxis in a non-conifer and is outside the claim's scope of cones. The pine-cone handedness literature reports counts only in papers, not as downloadable datasets I could fetch. I did not fetch any dataset landing page, so I am naming none rather than risk an unverified identifier.
